claim: Mesolimbic dopamine encoding of non-contingent rewards and reward-predictive cues has been well established.
source: Mesolimbic dopamine encoding of non-contingent rewards and reward-predictive cues has been well established.
evidence: This is a general statement about established scientific knowledge in the field, presented without specific data in this manuscript but as background context.

claim: Considerable debate remains over how mesolimbic dopamine responds to aversion and in the context of aversive conditioning.
source: Considerable debate remains over how mesolimbic dopamine responds to aversion and in the context of aversive conditioning.
evidence: This statement reflects ongoing scientific debate and is supported by the subsequent discussion of inconsistent findings in the literature.

claim: Pairing intraoral sucrose with malaise via injection of lithium chloride (LiCl) caused the development of a conditioned taste aversion (CTA).
source: Pairing intraoral sucrose with malaise via injection of lithium chloride (LiCl) caused the development of a conditioned taste aversion (CTA), which rendered the typically rewarding taste of sucrose aversive upon subsequent re-exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing behavioral and neural changes after LiCl pairing.

claim: Following CTA formation, intraoral sucrose suppressed the activity of ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons (VTADA).
source: Following CTA formation, intraoral sucrose suppressed the activity of ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons (VTADA) and nucleus accumbens (NAc) dopamine release.
evidence: This is directly supported by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 3G and related data.

claim: Following CTA formation, intraoral sucrose suppressed nucleus accumbens (NAc) dopamine release.
source: Following CTA formation, intraoral sucrose suppressed the activity of ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons (VTADA) and nucleus accumbens (NAc) dopamine release.
evidence: This is directly supported by fiber photometry recordings shown in Figure 3B and related data.

claim: The pattern of dopamine signaling after CTA is similar to intraoral infusions of innately aversive quinine.
source: This pattern of dopamine signaling after CTA is similar to intraoral infusions of innately aversive quinine and contrasts with responses to sucrose when it was novel or not paired with LiCl.
evidence: This comparison is supported by data in Figure 1 showing quinine responses and Figure 3 showing post-CTA sucrose responses.

claim: Dopamine responses were negatively correlated with behavioral reactivity to intraoral sucrose.
source: Dopamine responses were negatively correlated with behavioral reactivity to intraoral sucrose and predicted home cage sucrose preference.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figures 2, 4, and 9.

claim: Dopamine responses predicted home cage sucrose preference.
source: Dopamine responses were negatively correlated with behavioral reactivity to intraoral sucrose and predicted home cage sucrose preference.
evidence: This is supported by correlation data shown in Figures 6B and 9D.

claim: Dopamine responses scaled with the strength of the CTA, which was increased by repeated LiCl pairings.
source: Further, dopamine responses scaled with the strength of the CTA, which was increased by repeated LiCl pairings and weakened through extinction.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 showing effects of repeated conditioning.

claim: Dopamine responses scaled with the strength of the CTA, which was weakened through extinction.
source: Further, dopamine responses scaled with the strength of the CTA, which was increased by repeated LiCl pairings and weakened through extinction.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 5 and 8 showing recovery of dopamine responses during extinction.

claim: Dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTADA) and their release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) play key roles in the encoding of primary reward.
source: Dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTADA) and their release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) play key roles in the encoding of primary reward (Cohen et al., 2012; Roitman et al., 2008; Romo and Schultz, 1989), reward-related learning (Schultz, 2016; Schultz et al., 1997; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2017), and motivation (Berridge and Robinson, 1998; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Wise, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTADA) and their release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) play key roles in reward-related learning.
source: Dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTADA) and their release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) play key roles in the encoding of primary reward (Cohen et al., 2012; Roitman et al., 2008; Romo and Schultz, 1989), reward-related learning (Schultz, 2016; Schultz et al., 1997; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2017), and motivation (Berridge and Robinson, 1998; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Wise, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTADA) and their release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) play key roles in motivation.
source: Dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTADA) and their release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) play key roles in the encoding of primary reward (Cohen et al., 2012; Roitman et al., 2008; Romo and Schultz, 1989), reward-related learning (Schultz, 2016; Schultz et al., 1997; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2017), and motivation (Berridge and Robinson, 1998; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Wise, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Brief, phasic dopamine responses are evoked by primary rewarding stimuli and develop to their predictors.
source: Brief, phasic dopamine responses are evoked by primary rewarding stimuli and develop to their predictors (Konanur et al., 2024, for example).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Pauses in dopamine activity are evoked by reward omission.
source: Pauses in dopamine activity are evoked by reward omission (Sugam et al., 2012; Tobler et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some recordings of VTADA activity support increased signaling in aversion and aversive conditioning.
source: Some recordings of VTADA activity (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009) or dopamine release (Mikhailova et al., 2019; Wenzel et al., 2015) support increased signaling in aversion and aversive conditioning while others support decreased signaling (Mileykovskiy and Morales, 2011; Roitman et al., 2008; Ungless et al., 2004; Wheeler et al., 2011; Zhuo et al., 2024; see Morales and Margolis, 2017 for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing increased dopamine signaling.

claim: Some recordings of dopamine release support increased signaling in aversion and aversive conditioning.
source: Some recordings of VTADA activity (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009) or dopamine release (Mikhailova et al., 2019; Wenzel et al., 2015) support increased signaling in aversion and aversive conditioning while others support decreased signaling (Mileykovskiy and Morales, 2011; Roitman et al., 2008; Ungless et al., 2004; Wheeler et al., 2011; Zhuo et al., 2024; see Morales and Margolis, 2017 for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing increased dopamine release.

claim: Some recordings support decreased dopamine signaling in aversion and aversive conditioning.
source: Some recordings of VTADA activity (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009) or dopamine release (Mikhailova et al., 2019; Wenzel et al., 2015) support increased signaling in aversion and aversive conditioning while others support decreased signaling (Mileykovskiy and Morales, 2011; Roitman et al., 2008; Ungless et al., 2004; Wheeler et al., 2011; Zhuo et al., 2024; see Morales and Margolis, 2017 for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing decreased dopamine signaling.

claim: Aversion is a multi-dimensional construct that ranges from involuntary responses to noxious primary stimuli to passive or active avoidance in response to predictors of aversion.
source: First, like reward (Berridge and Robinson, 2003), aversion is a multi-dimensional construct that ranges from involuntary responses to noxious primary stimuli to passive or active avoidance in response to predictors of aversion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents established understanding in the field.

claim: Rewarding sweet and aversive bitter solutions activate different taste receptors.
source: Even when administering rewarding and aversive stimuli that utilize the same sensory pathway, as with taste, rewarding sweet and aversive bitter solutions activate different taste receptors (Schier and Spector, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Dopamine responses are modulated by physiological state (i.e., hunger, thirst, sodium appetite).
source: However, dopamine responses are modulated by physiological state (i.e., hunger, thirst, sodium appetite Cone et al., 2015; Fortin and Roitman, 2018; Hsu et al., 2020), presenting a further confound in interpreting mesolimbic responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: NAc lateral shell dopamine differentially encodes cues predictive of rewarding (i.e., sipper spout with sucrose) and aversive stimuli (i.e., footshock).
source: NAc lateral shell dopamine differentially encodes cues predictive of rewarding (i.e., sipper spout with sucrose) and aversive stimuli (i.e., footshock), which is distinct from other subregions (de Jong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Lithium chloride (LiCl) induces visceral malaise.
source: In Paired rats, the valence of sucrose was changed by subsequently administering lithium chloride (LiCl) – which induces visceral malaise (Bernstein et al., 1992) and reliably conditions a taste aversion (CTA; Garcia et al., 1 955; Garcia and Kimeldorf, 1957 ; Nachman and Ashe, 1973; Nolan et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2010; Swank and Bernstein, 1994; Thiele et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Lithium chloride (LiCl) reliably conditions a taste aversion (CTA).
source: In Paired rats, the valence of sucrose was changed by subsequently administering lithium chloride (LiCl) – which induces visceral malaise (Bernstein et al., 1992) and reliably conditions a taste aversion (CTA; Garcia et al., 1 955; Garcia and Kimeldorf, 1957 ; Nachman and Ashe, 1973; Nolan et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2010; Swank and Bernstein, 1994; Thiele et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Intraoral infusions of sucrose and quinine evoked different dopamine release responses in naive rats.
source: On average, intraoral infusions of sucrose and quinine evoked different dopamine release responses (t(5) = 3.61, p < 0.05; Figure 1C), which is consistent with prior work from our group (Hsu et al., 2020; Roitman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dopamine responses to sucrose and quinine delivery on individual trials were highly discriminable (area under the ROC curve [AUCROC] = 0.81).
source: Using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis (Cone et al., 2015; Green and Swets, 1974), we found dopamine responses to sucrose and quinine delivery on individual trials to be highly discriminable (area under the ROC curve [AUCROC] = 0.81; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Intraoral infusions of appetitive taste stimuli evoke mouth movements and tongue protrusions, but the head and body are relatively still.
source: Specifically, intraoral infusions of appetitive taste stimuli evoke mouth movements and tongue protrusions, but the head and body are relatively still.
evidence: This is based on established behavioral characterization cited from Grill and Norgren, 1978a.

claim: Aversive taste stimuli cause gapes, headshakes, forelimb flails, and chin rubs.
source: In contrast, aversive taste stimuli cause gapes, headshakes, forelimb flails, and chin rubs (Grill and Norgren, 1978a) – and, therefore, greater head and whole-body movement.
evidence: This is based on established behavioral characterization cited from Grill and Norgren, 1978a.

claim: Quinine produced greater average nose movement relative to sucrose in the same rats.
source: Quinine produced greater average nose (t(5) = 3.69, p < 0.05, Figure 2C); and forepaw (t(5) = 3.82, p < 0.05; Figure 2D) movement relative to sucrose in the same rats.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Quinine produced greater average forepaw movement relative to sucrose in the same rats.
source: Quinine produced greater average nose (t(5) = 3.69, p < 0.05, Figure 2C); and forepaw (t(5) = 3.82, p < 0.05; Figure 2D) movement relative to sucrose in the same rats.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Greater dopamine responses were associated with less movement evoked by the stimulus.
source: Importantly, these behavioral measures were negatively correlated to dopamine responses from the same rats where greater dopamine responses were associated with less movement evoked by the stimulus (nose movement to dopamine: r2 = 0.44, slope = −0.041; p < 0.05; forepaw moment to dopamine: r2 = 0.44, slope = −0.029; p < 0.05; Figure 2E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: In Unpaired rats, dopamine release to intraoral sucrose was unchanged between Conditioning Day and Test Day.
source: In Unpaired rats, dopamine release to intraoral sucrose was unchanged between days (Unpaired: t(9) = 0.83, p > 0.05; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In Paired rats, NAc dopamine release evoked by intraoral sucrose was significantly suppressed on Test Day relative to Conditioning Day.
source: In sharp contrast, in Paired rats NAc dopamine release evoked by intraoral sucrose was significantly suppressed on TD relative to CD (Paired: t(10) = 3.97, p < 0.005; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Dopamine release to intraoral sucrose on individual trials from Paired and Unpaired rats could not be discriminated on Conditioning Day (AUCROC = 0.50).
source: Using an ROC to test for between-subject differences, we found that dopamine release to intraoral sucrose on individual trials from Paired and Unpaired rats could not be discriminated on CD (AUCROC = 0.50) but could be well discriminated on TD (AUCROC = 0.80; Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figures 3C-F.

claim: Dopamine release to intraoral sucrose on individual trials from Paired and Unpaired rats could be well discriminated on Test Day (AUCROC = 0.80).
source: Using an ROC to test for between-subject differences, we found that dopamine release to intraoral sucrose on individual trials from Paired and Unpaired rats could not be discriminated on CD (AUCROC = 0.50) but could be well discriminated on TD (AUCROC = 0.80; Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figures 3C-F.

claim: VTADA activity was unchanged between days in Unpaired rats.
source: Similar to dopamine release in the NAc, VTADA activity was unchanged between days in Unpaired rats (Unpaired: t(5) = 0.60, p > 0.05; Figure 3G) but suppressed on TD relative to CD in Paired rats (Paired: t(6) = 2.627, p < 0.05; Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: VTADA activity was suppressed on Test Day relative to Conditioning Day in Paired rats.
source: Similar to dopamine release in the NAc, VTADA activity was unchanged between days in Unpaired rats (Unpaired: t(5) = 0.60, p > 0.05; Figure 3G) but suppressed on TD relative to CD in Paired rats (Paired: t(6) = 2.627, p < 0.05; Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Individual VTADA responses between groups could not be discriminated on Conditioning Day (AUCROC = 0.55).
source: Likewise, individual VTADA responses between groups could not be discriminated on CD (AUCROC = 0.55) but were well discriminated on TD (AUCROC = 0.76; Figure 3H–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figures 3H-K.

claim: Individual VTADA responses between groups were well discriminated on Test Day (AUCROC = 0.76).
source: Likewise, individual VTADA responses between groups could not be discriminated on CD (AUCROC = 0.55) but were well discriminated on TD (AUCROC = 0.76; Figure 3H–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figures 3H-K.

claim: In Unpaired rats, nose movement reactions were comparable between Conditioning Day and Test Day.
source: In the Unpaired rats, nose movement reactions were comparable between days (p > 0.05; Figure 4A) but Paired subjects showed increased nose movement to intraoral infusions from TD relative to CD (p = 0.0009; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Paired subjects showed increased nose movement to intraoral infusions from Test Day relative to Conditioning Day.
source: In the Unpaired rats, nose movement reactions were comparable between days (p > 0.05; Figure 4A) but Paired subjects showed increased nose movement to intraoral infusions from TD relative to CD (p = 0.0009; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Forepaw movement did not change from Conditioning Day to Test Day in Unpaired rats.
source: Forepaw movement did not change from CD to TD in Unpaired rats (p > 0.05; Figure 4B) but increased in Paired rats (p < 0.05; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Forepaw movement increased from Conditioning Day to Test Day in Paired rats.
source: Forepaw movement did not change from CD to TD in Unpaired rats (p > 0.05; Figure 4B) but increased in Paired rats (p < 0.05; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Paired rats showed greater forepaw reactivity than Unpaired rats on Test Day.
source: Further, Paired rats showed greater forepaw reactivity than Unpaired rats on TD (p < 0.01; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Dopamine release was negatively correlated with nose movement (r2 = 0.26, slope = −0.025, p < 0.001).
source: Examining the relationship between dopamine release and behavioral reactivity revealed negative correlations between dopamine release and nose movement (r2 = 0.26, slope = −0.025, p < 0.001; Figure 4C) and between dopamine release and forepaw moment (r2 = 0.22, slope = −0.021, p < 0.005; Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Dopamine release was negatively correlated with forepaw movement (r2 = 0.22, slope = −0.021, p < 0.005).
source: Examining the relationship between dopamine release and behavioral reactivity revealed negative correlations between dopamine release and nose movement (r2 = 0.26, slope = −0.025, p < 0.001; Figure 4C) and between dopamine release and forepaw moment (r2 = 0.22, slope = −0.021, p < 0.005; Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: VTADA activity was negatively correlated to nose movement (r2 = 0.48, slope = −0.057, p < 0.0005).
source: Further, dopamine activity was also negatively correlated to nose movement (r2 = 0.48, slope = −0.057, p < 0.0005; Figure 4G) and forepaw moment (r2 = 0.51, slope = −0.044, p < 0.0001; Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: VTADA activity was negatively correlated to forepaw movement (r2 = 0.51, slope = −0.044, p < 0.0001).
source: Further, dopamine activity was also negatively correlated to nose movement (r2 = 0.48, slope = −0.057, p < 0.0005; Figure 4G) and forepaw moment (r2 = 0.51, slope = −0.044, p < 0.0001; Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: A CTA can be extinguished when the conditioned stimulus (CS, i.e., intraoral sucrose) is repeatedly presented in the absence of the unconditioned stimulus (US, i.e., malaise induced by LiCl injection).
source: A CTA can be extinguished when the conditioned stimulus (CS, i.e., intraoral sucrose) is repeatedly presented in the absence of the unconditioned stimulus (US, i.e., malaise induced by LiCl injection) (Hadamitzky et al., 2015); however, it is unclear if CTA-suppressed dopamine responses to intraoral sucrose recover with extinction.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Intraoral sucrose infusions produced comparable VTADA activity responses in Unpaired rats across Conditioning Day and all Extinction days (E1–E5).
source: In a within-subjects comparison, intraoral sucrose infusions produced comparable VTADA activity responses in Unpaired rats across CD and all Extinction days (E1–E5, Unpaired: main effect of session: F(2.60,15.59) = 2.06, p > 0.05; Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: CTA formation suppressed sucrose-driven VTADA responses in Paired rats.
source: CTA formation suppressed sucrose-driven VTADA responses (Paired: CD vs. E1, p < 0.005; Figure 5B, C), but VTADA responses recovered to CD levels with re-exposure (Paired: CD vs. E2, p > 0.05; Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: VTADA responses recovered to Conditioning Day levels with re-exposure in Paired rats.
source: CTA formation suppressed sucrose-driven VTADA responses (Paired: CD vs. E1, p < 0.005; Figure 5B, C), but VTADA responses recovered to CD levels with re-exposure (Paired: CD vs. E2, p > 0.05; Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: VTADA responses to intraoral sucrose were discriminable on E1 (AUCROC = 0.76) and E2 (AUCROC = 0.77) between Unpaired and Paired groups.
source: VTADA responses to intraoral sucrose were discriminable on E1 (AUCROC = 0.76) and E2 (AUCROC = 0.77; Figure 5E, F) but not during E3–E5 (AUCROC ≤0.63).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: VTADA responses to intraoral sucrose were not discriminable during E3–E5 (AUCROC ≤0.63) between Unpaired and Paired groups.
source: VTADA responses to intraoral sucrose were discriminable on E1 (AUCROC = 0.76) and E2 (AUCROC = 0.77; Figure 5E, F) but not during E3–E5 (AUCROC ≤0.63).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: Paired rats had a significantly lower preference for sucrose on E1 relative to Unpaired rats.
source: Relative to Unpaired rats, Paired subjects had a significantly lower preference for sucrose on E1 (p < 0.0001; Figure 6A) and E2 (p < 0.0001; Figure 6A), which recovered to Unpaired levels by E3 (p > 0.05; Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of preference data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Paired rats had a significantly lower preference for sucrose on E2 relative to Unpaired rats.
source: Relative to Unpaired rats, Paired subjects had a significantly lower preference for sucrose on E1 (p < 0.0001; Figure 6A) and E2 (p < 0.0001; Figure 6A), which recovered to Unpaired levels by E3 (p > 0.05; Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of preference data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Sucrose preference recovered to Unpaired levels by E3 in Paired rats.
source: Relative to Unpaired rats, Paired subjects had a significantly lower preference for sucrose on E1 (p < 0.0001; Figure 6A) and E2 (p < 0.0001; Figure 6A), which recovered to Unpaired levels by E3 (p > 0.05; Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of preference data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Sucrose preference was predicted by VTADA responses to intraoral sucrose (r2 = 0.38, slope = 0.33, p < 0.0001).
source: Importantly, sucrose preference was predicted by the earlier recording of VTADA responses to intraoral sucrose (r2 = 0.38, slope = 0.33, p < 0.0001; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Intraoral sucrose evoked comparable VTADA responses in Unpaired rats between Conditioning Day and delayed Test Day.
source: Intraoral sucrose evoked comparable VTADA responses in Unpaired rats between CD and TD (Unpaired: t(4) = 0.97, p > 0.05; Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Dopamine responses were significantly suppressed in Paired rats on the delayed Test Day relative to Conditioning Day.
source: In contrast, dopamine responses were significantly suppressed in Paired rats on the delayed TD relative to CD (Paired: t(4) = 10.24, p = 0.0005; Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Individual VTADA responses to intraoral sucrose in Unpaired and Paired rats could not be discriminated on Conditioning Day (AUCROC = 0.59) in the delayed-test paradigm.
source: Further, while individual VTADA responses to intraoral sucrose in Unpaired and Paired rats could not be discriminated on CD (AUCROC = 0.59), they were well discriminated on TD (AUCROC = 0.84, Figure 7C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figures 7C-F.

claim: Individual VTADA responses to intraoral sucrose in Unpaired and Paired rats were well discriminated on delayed Test Day (AUCROC = 0.84).
source: Further, while individual VTADA responses to intraoral sucrose in Unpaired and Paired rats could not be discriminated on CD (AUCROC = 0.59), they were well discriminated on TD (AUCROC = 0.84, Figure 7C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figures 7C-F.

claim: Average VTADA activity was comparable across all Conditioning (C1–C3) and Extinction days (E1–E8) in Unpaired rats in the repeated-pairing paradigm.
source: In Unpaired rats, average VTADA activity was comparable across all Conditioning (C1–C3) and Extinction days (E1–E8, Unpaired: main effect of day: F(3.88,23.30) = 1.99, p > 0.05; Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 8B-D.

claim: Paired rats showed significant changes in VTADA responses to sucrose across the repeated-pairing paradigm.
source: In contrast, Paired rats showed significant changes in VTADA responses to sucrose across the paradigm (Paired: main effect of day: F(2.86,19.98) = 16.07, p < 0.0001; Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 8B-D.

claim: In Paired rats, VTADA responses were suppressed on C3 through E4 relative to C1.
source: In Paired rats, VTADA responses were suppressed on C3 through E4 (Paired: Relative to C1: C3–E4, p < 0.05; Figure 8B–D) but not subsequent Extinction days (Paired: Relative to C1: E5–E8, p > 0.05; Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 8B-D.

claim: Responses to intraoral sucrose were discriminable between Unpaired and Paired groups on C3 (AUCROC = 0.88).
source: Between-subject differences were also evident; responses to intraoral sucrose were discriminable between Unpaired and Paired groups on C3 (AUCROC = 0.88) and E1–E6 (AUCROC > 0.7; see Figure 8E–G for individual AUCROCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figures 8E-G.

claim: Responses to intraoral sucrose were discriminable between Unpaired and Paired groups on E1–E6 (AUCROC > 0.7).
source: Between-subject differences were also evident; responses to intraoral sucrose were discriminable between Unpaired and Paired groups on C3 (AUCROC = 0.88) and E1–E6 (AUCROC > 0.7; see Figure 8E–G for individual AUCROCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figures 8E-G.

claim: Intraoral sucrose delivery produced comparable behavioral responses in Unpaired rats across all days in the repeated-pairing paradigm.
source: Intraoral sucrose delivery produced comparable behavioral responses in Unpaired rats across all days (Unpaired: main effect of day: F(3.19,19.12) = 0.74, p > 0.05; Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Paired subjects showed shifts in behavioral responses across conditioning and extinction days in the repeated-pairing paradigm.
source: In contrast, Paired subjects showed shifts in behavioral responses across conditioning and extinction days (Paired: main effect of day: F(4.02,28.15) = 7.70, p = 0.0003; Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: VTADA activity and behavioral reactivity were negatively correlated across all rats and days (r2 = 0.43, slope = −9.52, p < 0.0001).
source: VTADA activity and behavioral reactivity were negatively correlated across all rats and days (r2 = 0.43, slope = −9.52, p < 0.0001; Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Paired rats had a lower sucrose preference on E1 through E5 compared to Unpaired rats in the repeated-pairing paradigm.
source: Specifically, Paired rats had a lower sucrose preference on E1 through E5 (E1 and E2 p < 0.0001, E3 p < 0.005, E4 p = 0.0001, E5 p < 0.05; Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of preference data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: VTADA responses were tightly correlated with post-session sucrose preference (r2 = 0.59, slope = 0.48, p < 0.0001).
source: Similar to behavioral reactivity but with more predictive power, VTADA responses were tightly correlated with post-session sucrose preference (r2 = 0.59, slope = 0.48, p < 0.0001; Figure 9D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Noxious stimuli have been reported to increase the firing rate of dopamine cell bodies in the VTA.
source: Noxious stimuli have been reported to increase the firing rate of dopamine cell bodies in the VTA (Anstrom et al., 2009; Anstrom and Woodward, 2005) and dopamine release in the NAc (Budygin et al., 2012; Kiyatkin, 1995; Mikhailova et al., 2019; Young, 2004; Young et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Noxious stimuli have been reported to increase dopamine release in the NAc.
source: Noxious stimuli have been reported to increase the firing rate of dopamine cell bodies in the VTA (Anstrom et al., 2009; Anstrom and Woodward, 2005) and dopamine release in the NAc (Budygin et al., 2012; Kiyatkin, 1995; Mikhailova et al., 2019; Young, 2004; Young et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Noxious stimuli have been reported to inhibit VTADA firing.
source: Conversely, others have reported that noxious stimuli inhibit VTADA firing (Brischoux et al., 2009; Ungless et al., 2004) and NAc dopamine release (Mantz et al., 1989; Wenzel et al., 2015) or that responses vary depending on the VTADA subpopulation or dopamine release site (Brischoux et al., 2009; de Jong et al., 2019; Zweifel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Noxious stimuli have been reported to inhibit NAc dopamine release.
source: Conversely, others have reported that noxious stimuli inhibit VTADA firing (Brischoux et al., 2009; Ungless et al., 2004) and NAc dopamine release (Mantz et al., 1989; Wenzel et al., 2015) or that responses vary depending on the VTADA subpopulation or dopamine release site (Brischoux et al., 2009; de Jong et al., 2019; Zweifel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Aversive stimuli can drive excitatory inputs to the VTA.
source: Aversive stimuli can drive excitatory inputs to the VTA (Amo et al., 2024; Faget et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Some reports indicate decreased dopamine responses to bitter quinine.
source: With respect to taste stimuli specifically, some reports indicate decreased (Roitman et al., 2008; Twining et al., 2015), while others report increased (Bassareo et al., 2002; Kutlu et al., 2021) dopamine responses to bitter quinine.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some reports indicate increased dopamine responses to bitter quinine.
source: With respect to taste stimuli specifically, some reports indicate decreased (Roitman et al., 2008; Twining et al., 2015), while others report increased (Bassareo et al., 2002; Kutlu et al., 2021) dopamine responses to bitter quinine.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neuroanatomical data support projections to the VTA from relatively early nodes of the gustatory pathway (e.g., parabrachial nucleus; PBN).
source: Neuroanatomical data support projections to the VTA from relatively early nodes of the gustatory pathway (e.g., parabrachial nucleus; PBN) and specifically sucrose and quinine-responsive neurons in the PBN (Boughter et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Recent work has supported dopamine alignment with the encoding of stimulus salience.
source: Indeed, recent work has supported dopamine alignment with the encoding of stimulus salience (Chen and Bruchas, 2021; Kutlu et al., 2021) to contribute to prioritizing attentional processes toward stimuli of high intensity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Human VTA activation is greater for novel, more highly salient stimuli than to familiar stimuli.
source: Further, human VTA activation is greater for novel, more highly salient stimuli than to familiar stimuli (Bunzeck and Düzel, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Local GABA neurons innervate and suppress VTADA neurons through neurotransmission at GABAA receptors.
source: Local GABA neurons innervate and suppress VTADA neurons through neurotransmission at GABAA receptors, which can pause VTADA activity and downstream dopamine release in the NAc (Mathon et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Decreases in dopamine activity can lead to an uncoupling of dopamine and high-affinity dopamine D2-like receptors expressed on medium spiny neurons.
source: Decreases in dopamine activity can lead to an uncoupling of dopamine and high-affinity dopamine D2-like receptors expressed on medium spiny neurons (Dreyer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Manipulations of NAc activity can influence taste reactivity.
source: As manipulations of NAc activity can influence taste reactivity (Morales and Berridge, 2020), differential dopamine responses to sucrose in rats with versus without CTA likely applies a critical filter for NAc processing in the service of oromotor output.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Other aversive conditioning paradigms have shown development of decreased dopamine responses to cues predictive of primary aversive stimuli.
source: Other aversive conditioning paradigms have shown development of decreased dopamine responses to cues predictive of primary aversive stimuli (Goedhoop et al., 2022; Zhuo et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CTA can form with just one taste–illness pairing.
source: As we've shown here, CTA can form with just one taste–illness pairing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 3).

claim: The PBN is essential for CTA formation.
source: The PBN is essential for CTA formation (Spector et al., 1992) and contains neurons that process gustatory and illness information (Carter et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The PBN contains neurons that process gustatory and illness information.
source: The PBN is essential for CTA formation (Spector et al., 1992) and contains neurons that process gustatory and illness information (Carter et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The amygdala is critical for CTA acquisition.
source: The amygdala is also critical for CTA acquisition (Gao et al., 2023; Inui et al., 2019; Morin et al., 2021; Morris et al., 1999; St. Andre and Reilly, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The same neurons within the basolateral nucleus of the amygdala are responsive to both novel taste and LiCl.
source: The same neurons within the basolateral nucleus of the amygdala are responsive to both novel taste and LiCl (Barot et al., 2008; Zimmerman et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The rostral tegmental nucleus (RMTg) is a robust source of GABAergic input onto VTADA neurons and suppresses their firing.
source: The rostral tegmental nucleus (RMTg) is a robust source of GABAergic input onto VTADA neurons and suppresses their firing (Balcita-Pedicino et al., 2011; Bourdy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Primary aversive stimuli, including LiCl, increase RMTg neuronal firing.
source: Primary aversive stimuli, including LiCl, increase RMTg neuronal firing (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Re-exposure to LiCl-paired saccharin increases cFos expression in the RMTg.
source: Further, re-exposure to LiCl-paired saccharin increases cFos expression in the RMTg (Glover et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: LiCl injections suppress electrically evoked NAc dopamine release.
source: Likewise, LiCl injections suppress electrically evoked NAc dopamine release (Fortin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Multiple conditioning trials caused greater suppression in dopamine activity evoked by the sucrose CS.
source: Multiple conditioning trials caused greater suppression in dopamine activity evoked by the sucrose CS. This has been previously reported for audiovisual cues that predict discrete, noxious stimuli (e.g., air puff Zhuo et al., 2024 and foot shock Wilkinson et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 8 and citations to prior literature.

claim: Taste, relative to other sensory stimuli, serves as a uniquely strong predictor for illness.
source: Taste, relative to other sensory stimuli, serves as a uniquely strong predictor for illness (Garcia and Koelling, 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to classic literature.

claim: Repeated re-exposure to the conditioned stimulus without subsequent malaise drives CTA extinction.
source: After establishing CTA, repeated re-exposure to the conditioned stimulus without subsequent malaise drives CTA extinction (Cantora et al., 2006; Mickley et al., 2004; Nolan et al., 1997), allowing for new, contextual knowledge to conflict with the original association between the taste and negative post-ingestive outcome (Bouton and Bolles, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The infralimbic (IL) cortex plays a role in extinction learning.
source: The infralimbic (IL) cortex plays a role in extinction learning (Quirk et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Stimulation of the IL suppresses aversive taste reactivity to sucrose after it had been paired with LiCl.
source: Stimulation of the IL suppresses aversive taste reactivity to sucrose after it had been paired with LiCl (Hurley and Carelli, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There is considerable heterogeneity among dopamine neurons.
source: It is important to recognize that there is considerable heterogeneity among dopamine neurons (Phillips et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: VTA neurons that release both glutamate and dopamine are important for aversion.
source: Indeed, VTA neurons that release both glutamate and dopamine are important for aversion, and it is the dopamine signal from these neurons that is critical for this process (Warlow et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: A range of clinically used drugs – from anti-obesity treatments to chemotherapeutics – induce malaise and can lead to the development of CTAs and a reduction in motivation.
source: A range of clinically used drugs – from anti-obesity treatments to chemotherapeutics – induce malaise and can lead to the development of CTAs and a reduction in motivation.
evidence: This is a general statement about clinical implications based on established knowledge.

source: Male and female (intact, naturally cycling) Long Evans rats (>250 g) were bred from females heterozygous for expressing Cre recombinase under the control of the tyrosine hydroxylase promoter (TH:Cre) (Rat Research Resource Center, RRRC No. 659; Witten et al., 2011) and male wildtype rats (Charles River Laboratories).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

evidence: This describes the experimental design.

evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

source: To overcome these limitations, we measured lateral VTADA neural activity and dopamine release in the lateral shell of the NAc using fiber photometry as we varied the valence of intraoral sucrose infusions.

evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

source: To assay the stereotypical appetitive and aversive behavioral responses to taste stimuli (Breslin et al., 1992; Grill and Norgren, 1978a), we used a deep-learning algorithm (DeepLabCut, Mathis et al., 2018) and home cage sucrose preference task to assess the valence of intraoral sucrose.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The mesolimbic dopamine system differentially encodes valence – reward versus aversion – and flexibly for the same stimulus.
source: Thus, we conclude that the mesolimbic dopamine system differentially encodes valence – reward versus aversion – and flexibly for the same stimulus.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.
